Paseah
pa-sē′ah
n. (a man of Judah; also a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylon, one of whose sons repaired the Old Gate)
Hebrew Pase'ach, from pasach (H6452), to limp, to pass over, to hop; the same root that gives Pesach, Passover. Nehemiah’s Nethinim list spells the family name Phaseah at the corresponding place.

Biblical Definition

The name belongs first to a man of Judah in the Chronicler’s genealogy: “And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah” (1 Chronicles 4:12). A family bearing the same name is counted among the Nethinim, the temple servants, who returned with Zerubbabel: “The children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai” (Ezra 2:49). At the same place in Nehemiah’s independent register the family is spelled Phaseah: “The children of Gazzam, the children of Uzza, the children of Phaseah” (Nehemiah 7:51). A son of this returned house did not stay a name on a list; he took up a trowel: “Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah” (Nehemiah 3:6). The name’s own root, pasach, to limp or to pass over, is the same verb behind Pesach, the Passover, the night the LORD passed over the houses marked by blood. A family named from limping and passing over spent its strength, generations later, rebuilding the very gates of the city the LORD had once passed over in judgment and mercy both.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) has no entry for Paseah; the name is built on the Hebrew verb for limping or passing over, the same root behind Passover, and belongs to a man of Judah and to a family of Nethinim whose son helped rebuild Jerusalem’s wall.

PASEAH, n. A man of Judah; also a family of Nethinim who returned from Babylonian captivity.

PASSOVER, n. A feast of the Jews, instituted to commemorate the exemption of the Israelites in Egypt.

GATE, n. A large door, or entrance into a city, castle, or other large edifice.

REPAIR, v.t. To restore to a sound or good state after decay, injury, or partial destruction.

NETHINIM, n. Temple servants given by the congregation of Israel to assist the Levites.

Key Scripture

1 Chronicles 4:12 — "And Eshton begat Bethrapha, and Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Irnahash. These are the men of Rechah."

Ezra 2:49 — "The children of Uzza, the children of Paseah, the children of Besai,"

Nehemiah 3:6 — "Moreover the old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah, and Meshullam the son of Besodeiah; they laid the beams thereof, and set up the doors thereof, and the locks thereof, and the bars thereof."

Nehemiah 7:51 — "The children of Gazzam, the children of Uzza, the children of Phaseah,"

Modern Corruption

The two spellings, Paseah and Phaseah, are sometimes cited as evidence of an unreliable text; read plainly they are ordinary orthographic variation within a single language across two independently copied books, exactly as the same name is spelled two ways in a modern family Bible's flyleaf.

expand to see more

A skeptical reading of the historical books treats every spelling difference as a wound in the text’s reliability, building toward the conclusion that Scripture cannot be trusted in its details because it is not perfectly uniform in its details. But perfect uniformity of spelling was never the promise; verbal plenary inspiration guarantees that what the human authors wrote down was exactly what the Spirit intended asserted, and two faithful scribes rendering one Hebrew name with or without an initial letter is precisely the kind of variation that honest, independent transmission produces.

The name itself faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is in the root: a name built on limping and on passing over became, in Jehoiada son of Paseah, a name attached to a repaired gate. The LORD who passed over Israel in Egypt is the same LORD whose gates a limping people’s sons were given strength to rebuild.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew pasach (H6452), to limp, to pass over; Pesach (H6453), Passover; sha'ar (H8179), gate; chazaq (H2388), to repair, to make strong.

expand to see more

Hebrew pasach (H6452) — to limp, to hop, to pass over; the root of the name Paseah.

Hebrew Pesach (H6453) — Passover; the feast built on the same root.

Hebrew sha'ar (H8179) — gate; the old gate Jehoiada son of Paseah repaired.

Hebrew chazaq (H2388) — to repair, to strengthen, to make firm.

Hebrew Nethinim (H5411) — those given; the temple servants Paseah’s house was numbered among.

Usage

"“Paseah…These are the men of Rechah” — the name in Judah’s genealogy."

"“The children of Paseah” — the returning Nethinim household."

"“The old gate repaired Jehoiada the son of Paseah” — the name at work on the wall."
